title: The Papers: 'Future looking droughtful' and 'Dinghy flotilla'
originalTitle: The Papers: 'Future looking droughtful' and 'Dinghy flotilla'
content:
The Times, external says that some of England's metro mayors could hand money back to residents under the prime minister's devolution plans. The paper says the policy is being framed as a way to boost investment in public services and infrastructure but some Conservative and Reform UK mayors are instead planning to use fiscal devolution to lower the tax burden for their voters.

The Daily Mail, external and the Sun, external both have very similar front pages showing migrants crammed on to dinghies off the coast of France, noting that just a day earlier, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the plan to stop small boats was effective. "Still say your boats plan is working, Andy?" asks the Mail. The Sun quotes a French police officer, watching a boat setting off, as saying, "Our orders are to let them go."

The Sun, external says a British Airways passenger jet stalled about 4,000ft over London in "the most serious near miss in the UK for years". The paper understands the captain is grounded on stress leave after having to intervene to save the plane. BA is quoted as saying it is assisting the air accident investigation.

The Daily Telegraph, external says calls are growing for England to boycott the next World Cup over the Fifa president Gianni Infantino's plan to sell stakes in the competition to private investors. The paper says that if Infantino does not come to his senses, Uefa and the FA should withdraw from the organisation. Without their involvement, it says, there could be no World Cup worthy of the name. The Daily Mirror, external says Infantino promised to clean up Fifa. Instead, it concludes, he risks being remembered as the man who Americanised the World Cup and tried to sell football's crown jewels.

"The last laugh" is the Times's , externalheadline as it reports that the BBC is axing the comedy show Live at the Apollo after more than two decades, alongside Blankety Blank and Celebrity Mastermind. Ditching much-loved shows, warns the Daily Express, external, means the BBC's future will become even more precarious.
